name: Achaemenid Empire (Darius III)

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 3.8-4.325 million km2 for 450-331 BCE (low, mid). The historical-basemaps world_bc400 polygon measures 6.02 million km2 on the sphere (computed from the GeoJSON, high); it includes Egypt and the nominal Indus and Central Asian satrapies.

population.note: Seshat codes 20-26 million for 500 BCE and 17-35 million for 400 BCE (range used). Egypt, in revolt 404-343, was reconquered by Artaxerxes III and is counted. Everything inside the imperial border, including Egypt, Babylonia, Anatolia, Bactria and the eastern satrapies.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Seshat (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/107) codes the largest settlement at 200,000 (Babylon) for 550-331 BCE. Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Levant and western Anatolia urbanised; the Iranian plateau and Central Asia much less. Same as persia-achaemenid--480.

activePersonnel.note: Field forces of 334-333 (57,000 / 110,000 / 200,000, see forces) + fleet crews (60,000 / 70,000 / 80,000, see supportPersonnel) + garrisons left across the empire (40,000 / 60,000 / 100,000; educated guess: satrapal guards, citadels such as Sardis, Babylon, Memphis, Elephantine, and the eastern satrapies that sent troops only for Gaugamela). Convention: satrapal contingents already assembled for the 334-333 campaigns, garrisons and fleet crews are counted as active; eastern levies that joined only in 331 are in trainedReserves.

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Iranian and eastern cavalry and levies (Bactrians, Saka, Arachosians) that reached the royal army only in 331 for Gaugamela; reachable within ~30 days only from the western satrapies.

supportPersonnel.note: Fleet crews: 300 / 350 / 400 warships (see ships_major) x ~200 men (oarsmen, deck crew, marines). Excludes transports, the royal baggage train and court.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Agrarian empire levying satrapal contingents and military colonists; the 334-333 field forces plus fleet were already ~0.7% of the population. Same convention as persia-achaemenid--480.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Line infantry = Greek mercenary hoplites (Arrian: ~20,000 at the Granicus, 30,000 at Issus; modern estimates mostly 10,000-20,000 in total) + kardakes and Persian spearmen including the 1,000 apple-bearer guards (Arrian 2.8.6 gives 60,000 kardakes, rejected). Mid 20,000 mercenaries + 20,000 Iranian line infantry.

quality.note: Greek mercenary hoplite panoply era-typical (0.5) to good; kardakes lighter. No sarissa phalanx.

training.note: Greek mercenaries professional (0.75); kardakes semi-trained young Persians (0.5).

count.note: Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Archers and slingers of the satrapal and royal levies ~27% of the field force.

quality.note: Composite bows and wicker shields, little armour; era-typical missile troops but outranged by nothing and outclassed in close combat (rubric 0.5).

count.note: Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Javelinmen and hill levies (Arrian 2.8.5: 20,000 light-armed sent across the Pinarus) ~14%.

Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Armoured Iranian noble and royal kinsmen cavalry, Bactrian and Hyrcanian heavy horse; the Persian army's main arm (Arrian: ~20,000 horse at the Granicus, 30,000 at Issus) ~40% of the cavalry.

quality.note: Scale-armoured riders with javelins and short spears, horse armour for some (Xenophon's cavalry ideal); good but outmatched by the Companions' xyston in close combat.

count.note: Field forces of 334-333 = the western satrapal army met at the Granicus (May 334) plus the royal army mustered at Babylon for Issus (Nov 333). Livius (https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/) puts Darius' army at Issus at about 100,000 men; Arrian 2.8.5-8 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_II/Chapter_VIII) gives 600,000, Arrian 1.14.4 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XIV) ~20,000 cavalry and nearly 20,000 Greek mercenaries at the Granicus (ancient figures, not used as mid). Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (isbn:0521343208, ch. 3) reduces both armies sharply. Total land field force: low 57,000, mid 110,000, high 200,000; split by role below. Light horse and mounted archers (Saka, Dahae, Medes, satrapal horse) ~60% of the cavalry.

training.note: Iranian and steppe riders raised in the saddle.

count.note: Educated guess. Scythed chariots were part of the royal army (200 at Gaugamela 331 per Arrian 3.8.6, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_III/Chapter_VIII, ancient); none at the Granicus or Issus. Number on hand in 334 unknown.

quality.note: Scythed chariots were defeated by opening lanes at Gaugamela; below era-typical.

count.note: Arrian 1.18.5 (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Anabasis_of_Alexander/Book_I/Chapter_XVIII) gives about 400 Persian ships at Miletus in summer 334 against Nicanor's 160 (ancient figure, high). Mid 350 allows for undermanned or detached ships; Phoenician, Cypriot and Cilician triremes with some larger polyremes. Disintegrated in 333-332 when Alexander took the Phoenician bases.

quality.note: Phoenician and Cypriot ships among the era's best (rubric 0.75); Arrian 1.18 has Alexander refuse battle with the "disciplined fleet of the Cyprians and Phoenicians".

training.note: Professional Phoenician and Cypriot seafarers; Memnon an able commander.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: divided satrapal command at the Granicus (Memnon's scorched-earth advice rejected), Darius III an average-to-poor field commander; strong staff for musters and logistics. Memnon competent at sea.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: multi-ethnic host plus mercenaries; core Persian guard and cavalry better.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5 average; the empire had just suppressed Egypt (343) but faced court turmoil (Bagoas, accession of Darius III in 336).

weapons.note: Close to anchor 3 (300 BCE: iron weapons, torsion artillery): iron weapons general, Greek mercenary hoplites; torsion artillery used defensively at Halicarnassus but no sarissa.

armor.note: Anchor 2-3: scale and linen armour for elites and mercenaries, many levies unarmoured.

ships.note: Anchor 3: triremes plus early quadriremes and quinqueremes in the Phoenician and Cypriot squadrons.

fortification.note: Anchor 3: ashlar city walls (Tyre, Halicarnassus, Babylon) able to resist Macedonian siege towers for months.

logistics.note: Anchor 3 plus: Royal Road and depot system documented in the Persepolis Fortification tablets (Briant, isbn:1575060310, ch. 9); huge treasuries. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.1 -> 2.97, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for -334 (2.969); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

communications.note: Anchor 3: mounted relay posts (angareion) on the royal roads. audit 2026-10-30: mid 3.1 -> 2.97, capped at the SOURCES.md tech anchor interpolated for -334 (2.969); the mid may not exceed the anchor for its year.

isr.note: Year anchor 3: mounted scouts and spies; before Issus the two armies passed each other on opposite sides of the Amanus without either detecting the other (Livius, https://www.livius.org/articles/battle/issus/).

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: year 1 CE values for Iran, Iraq, Egypt, Israel and Jordan are 1,116, Turkey 897 (2011 int$). Applied to the empire three centuries earlier with a wider range; Central Asian and plateau satrapies were poorer than Mesopotamia and Egypt. Same convention as persia-achaemenid--480.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Most service still paid in land grants (hatru) and satrapal levies, but mercenary armies were paid in coin; Alexander later found ~120,000 talents at Persepolis (Diodorus 17.71, ancient), showing that much revenue was hoarded rather than spent.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Agrarian empire with craft centres in Mesopotamia, Egypt, Phoenicia and Lydia.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Irrigated Mesopotamian and Egyptian agriculture produced large surpluses stored in royal granaries.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in an ancient Greek-type age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model used for all classical and medieval snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Sardis-Susa Royal Road ~2,500 km (Herodotus 5.52-53) is the low bound; the Persepolis tablets attest further royal routes to Persepolis, Ecbatana, Bactra, Arachosia and Egypt (Briant, isbn:1575060310, ch. 9). Same as persia-achaemenid--480.

majorPorts.note: Phoenicia (Sidon, Tyre, Arwad, Byblos), Cyprus (Salamis), Cilicia, Egypt, Ionia and Caria; count of ports able to supply a fleet is an estimate by analogy with persia-achaemenid--480.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Phoenician and Egyptian merchant shipping; same order as persia-achaemenid--480.

supplyRangeKm.note: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander, ch. 9: Persian armies moved along royal roads with pre-stocked depots and a huge baggage train (Darius left his at Damascus before Issus); away from roads and depots the range was short. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. ~0.07 / 0.09 / 0.11 draft and pack animals (incl. camels) per inhabitant x population.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2 (local supply, fortified cities); deep strategic depth and desert climate argue for 1.3, weak loyalty of subject peoples (Egypt welcomed Alexander) for less.

notes: Snapshot = spring 334 BCE, Alexander crossing the Hellespont. Forces are the field forces the empire put into the field in 334-333 (the Granicus satrapal army and the royal army mustered for Issus), not a single simultaneous order of battle; garrisons are in activePersonnel only. Arrian's figures (600,000 at Issus, 1,040,000 at Gaugamela, 400 ships) are cited in notes but not used as mid values except the ship count, which modern historians broadly accept. The 15 Indian elephants at Gaugamela (Arrian 3.8.6) arrived only in 331 and are not counted. Population convention: everything inside the bc400 polygon, Seshat range; Egypt (reconquered 343) included.
